title: The Ground Before Hyde Park
voiceover: Start where Hyde Park starts. Not with street numbers. With prairie and marsh, sloping down to the lake. Sand ridges hold bur oaks. Swales hold wildflowers. The grassland runs flat to the horizon. The water sits close, and the ground stays wet most of the year. And people already live here. The Potawatomi hold this land in common with the Ojibwe and the Odawa, an alliance they call the Council of Three Fires. One elder, reading the old scrolls, traces that council back to the 790s, near the straits of Michilimackinac. The three nations split the work. The Ojibwe keep the faith. The Odawa keep the trade. The Potawatomi keep the fire. They hunt, trade, and live along these shores for generations, long before any deed exists to describe them. The water is what draws outsiders in. A few miles northwest runs the Chicago Portage, a low seven-mile stretch of wet ground that floods into a shallow basin the traders call Mud Lake. In a wet season, a canoe floats almost from the Great Lakes to the Mississippi. Only a short carry separates the two watersheds. People work that crossing for centuries. Then, in the summer of 1673, Kaskaskia guides lead a French fur trader, Louis Jolliet, and a Jesuit priest, Jacques Marquette, back up the Illinois and the Des Plaines and over the portage. They become the first Europeans known to stand on the site of Chicago. Jolliet sees it at once. One short canal could join the lake to the river, and the whole interior of the continent to the sea. Digging it would take 175 years. Say the city's name and you are speaking a word for an onion. Chicago is a French spelling of shikaakwa, a Miami-Illinois word for the wild leek that grew thick in the river bottoms. In 1687 one of La Salle's men wrote that people called the place Chicagou because of the quantity of wild garlic in the woods. The city is named for an onion.  The United States arrived as a garrison. In 1803, soldiers under Captain John Whistler built Fort Dearborn at the mouth of the river. A sandbar shaped like an elephant's trunk blocked the harbor, so the river bent south and ran parallel to the lake before it found a way out. Ships anchored offshore and waited. The garrison never held the ground easily. In 1812 the soldiers abandoned the fort, Potawatomi fighters attacked the column as it left, and the place burned, then rebuilt four years later. For most of three decades that lone fort was nearly all that passed for a town.  The land changed hands on paper first. In 1816, at Portage des Sioux on the Mississippi, the same Three Fires nations signed the Treaty of St. Louis and ceded a strip about twenty miles wide, running from the lake to the Illinois River, the exact ground a canal would need. Surveyors drew it as the Indian Boundary Line. A few Chicago streets still run that old diagonal today, cutting across the grid, because they trace a line that predates the grid. And the men who wanted that canal corridor had only begun. The land here emptied partly because of a war the Potawatomi never fought. It started with lead. After miners struck ore around Galena in the 1820s, they poured onto ground the Sauk and Meskwaki still farmed and shoved them west of the Mississippi. Black Hawk would not stay shoved. In the spring of 1832, the sixty-five-year-old Sauk leader led about a thousand Sauk, Meskwaki, and Kickapoo back across the river, most of them women and children, to plant corn on land a disputed 1804 treaty had signed away. Black Hawk and others called that treaty worthless. The men who signed it, he said, never had the right to sell. Illinois settlers raised a militia anyway. The Black Hawk War ran from April to August. It ended on the second of August at the mouth of the Bad Axe River in Wisconsin, where soldiers and militia opened fire on people waving a white flag, trying to surrender. A thousand had crossed in spring. Roughly a hundred and fifty lived to see the fall. The war was short, and the government read its lesson plainly. Native nations that stayed could be removed, and the Northwest thrown open to settlers. The Indian Removal Act of 1830 had already written that into law. Now the army had proven it could be done. No battle took this ground. A signature did. On the twenty-sixth of September, 1833, federal commissioners called thousands of Potawatomi, Ojibwe, and Odawa to Chicago and pressed them to sign. The talks dragged on for weeks. Many of the chiefs refused to sell, and the men who finally marked the paper did not all speak for the people that paper would bind. One document swept it away. The Three Fires nations gave up about five million acres across Illinois and the Michigan Territory, this lakefront among them. In return the government promised five million acres west of the Mississippi, a hundred thousand dollars in goods, fourteen thousand dollars in cash a year for twenty years, money for mills and farm tools, and seventy thousand dollars for schools. The Potawatomi got three years to leave. Witnesses recorded what the leaving looked like. In August 1835, around five thousand Potawatomi gathered at the agency house for their last annuity payment. About eight hundred men rose and danced through the streets of Chicago. They had roached their hair and tied hawk and eagle feathers nearly to the ground. They painted their faces red and black, the foreheads, cheeks, and noses ridged with curved stripes edged in points. They moved from the council house west along the river. They stopped before every house they passed, crossed the north branch, and were gone. John Caton, a young lawyer who would later sit on the Illinois Supreme Court, watched and called it a war dance. The dancers knew it as something else. Caton himself wrote that they understood it as the last dance on their native soil, a kind of funeral for old associations and memories. The funeral was for the living. The removal had only begun. Removal did not happen in a single day. It dragged on for years, and it kept finding crueler forms. The worst came in 1838, when Chicago itself was already a city. That year, militia forced about 859 Potawatomi out of Indiana and marched them to eastern Kansas. The march began at Twin Lakes, near Plymouth, Indiana. It ended on the fourth of November along the Osage River, near present-day Osawatomie. The route ran roughly 660 miles over 61 days. People died as they walked. More than forty died on the way, most of them children, of typhoid and exhaustion. A young priest, Father Benjamin Petit, walked the whole distance beside them and kept a journal. The march broke him too. He died the next year in St. Louis, at twenty-seven. History remembers that march as the Trail of Death. They scattered the Potawatomi. They did not erase them. The bands they marched to Kansas became the Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation. In 2024 the Prairie Band won back a piece of its ancestral ground at Shabbona, placed in trust, and became the first federally recognized tribe to hold land in Illinois again. And one band never left. Chief Leopold Pokagon kept about 280 people in southwestern Michigan, and by 1838 they had bought 874 acres of their own land near Dowagiac. Their descendants are the Pokagon Band of Potawatomi, more than six thousand citizens today. The people who held this lakefront are still here. Now the land sat legally cleared, and the city at the river mouth took off. Chicago incorporated as a town in 1833, the same year as the treaty, with about three hundred residents. By 1837 it was a city of more than four thousand. Soldiers cut a channel straight through the sandbar and finally gave the river a real harbor. Speculators bought the wet lots and flipped them faster than anyone could build, until the panic of 1837 wiped out the easy money and a good many of the speculators with it. The land had emptied. The lakefront that became Hyde Park stayed empty a while longer. The same sand that turned the portage into a crossing made this ground poor for crops. Nathan Watson learned that the hard way. He tried to farm a stretch near the Chicago-to-Detroit wagon road, around what is now 53rd Street and Lake Park. That road was not new. It followed the old Sauk Trail, the Native footpath that ran from the Mississippi at Rock Island east to the Detroit River, the same kind of trail the Potawatomi had walked for generations before a surveyor ever touched it. Watson dreamed of an orchard. The sand beat him. So he turned his place into a tavern and fed the travelers passing through. When he died, his widow, Electa Watson, ran it as a boarding house and farm, the only real structure for miles along that shore. The same country still surrounded it. Sand ridges with bur oaks, swales of wildflowers, prairie to the horizon. A young lawyer rode straight into that country in 1853. Paul Cornell came six miles south from the city most mornings just to buy a glass of buttermilk from Electa Watson at the tavern. That August he gambled. He bought three hundred acres of lakefront that no one else wanted and sank nearly everything he had into the sand. He named the place Hyde Park, after the London park. Within a few years he deeded sixty of those acres to the Illinois Central Railroad and won a depot at 53rd Street and a promise of daily trains to the city. The grocery clerks, the elevated trains, the university all lay decades off. The bur oaks and the wildflowers already stood there. So did the deed, passed from a tavern keeper's widow to a man with a plan. The first taking had set the pattern. Whoever held the paper would claim this ground, clear it, and remake it, again and again.

beats.heading: Prairie and Marsh
beats.anchor: there was prairie and marsh sloping down to the lake

beats.heading: The Black Hawk War
beats.anchor: a sixty-five-year-old Sauk leader named Black Hawk led about a thousand Sauk, Meskwaki, and Kickapoo people
beats.text: The pressure that emptied the rest of the land came partly from a war the Potawatomi did not fight. beats.visual: Period map of the Northwest Territory shading the lands opened to settlement after 1832; an on-screen line noting the Indian Removal Act of 1830 as the governing policy.

beats.heading: The Trail of Death
beats.anchor: militia forced about 859 Potawatomi out of Indiana and marched them to eastern Kansas
beats.text: Removal was not one event. It ran for years and bent in cruel directions. The hardest came in 1838, after Chicago itself was already a city, when militia forced about 859 Potawatomi out of Indiana and marched them to eastern Kansas. The march began at Twin Lakes, near Plymouth, Indiana, and ended on the fourth of November along the Osage River, near present-day Osawatomie. The route ran roughly 660 miles over 61 days. More than forty people died on the way, most of them children, of typhoid and exhaustion. A young priest, Father Benjamin Petit, walked the whole distance with them and kept a journal. beats.visual: Route map of the 1838 Trail of Death from Twin Lakes, Indiana to Osawatomie, Kansas; a stat card (859 removed, 660 miles, 61 days, 40+ dead); portrait or marker image of Father Benjamin Petit.

beats.heading: Scattered, Not Erased
beats.anchor: The Potawatomi were scattered, not erased
beats.text: The Potawatomi were scattered, not erased. The bands that were marched to Kansas became the Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation, which in 2024 had a piece of its ancestral ground at Shabbona placed back in trust and became the first federally recognized tribe with land in Illinois. One band never left at all. Chief Leopold Pokagon kept about 280 people in southwestern Michigan, and by 1838 they had bought 874 acres of their own land near Dowagiac. Their descendants are the Pokagon Band of Potawatomi, more than six thousand citizens today. The people who held this lakefront are still here.
beats.visual: Present-day images of the Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation and the 2024 Shabbona land restoration (WTTW/Capitol News Illinois coverage); a map of the federally recognized Potawatomi nations today; a card with citizen counts (Pokagon Band 6,000+).
